components.label: What they call the planning step
What they call the working step
A person approves or edits first
How it keeps going until it passes
Names reuse, risks or breaking changes

plan-name.name: Ask Devin
plan-name.summary: The docs page says to use Ask Devin to ask questions about your codebase, plan tasks, and generate high-context sessions. The page does not mention the !plan playbook.

execute-name.name: Devin session
execute-name.summary: The docs tell people to start one Devin session for each verifiable sub-task, so the session is the unit in which Devin works a task.

plan-hitl.omitted: Pages checked: Ask Devin, Linear, Jira, Using Playbooks, gallery bulk-plan-backlog and prd-to-tickets (docs.devin.ai). They describe a person working with Devin in conversation or Devin posting plan comments with open questions, but none states whether a person must approve or edit the plan before work starts.

plan-persist.name: PRD to tickets
plan-persist.summary: In the gallery example Devin reads a PRD and creates Linear tickets, so the plan lives in the tracker. The bulk-plan example instead posts the plan as a comment on each ticket. Ask Devin produces a prompt that starts a session; the page does not say it is saved.
plan-persist.short: Yes: Linear tickets and ticket comments

plan-contents.name: PRD to tickets
plan-contents.summary: The page's example output is tickets with an ID, title, T-shirt size, dependencies on other tickets, description, acceptance criteria and likely file paths; it is an example, not a guaranteed format. The Ask Devin page does not say its breakdown carries criteria or dependencies.
plan-contents.short: Mixed: example tickets carry both; Ask Devin unstated

verify-judge.name: unknown
verify-judge.summary: Devin runs existing tests, lint and type checks in its own environment before submitting a PR. Which checks run is set by the prompt, playbook or repo skill, not by a fixed pipeline.

verify-runs-app.name: Testing mode
verify-runs-app.summary: After a PR is created Devin can enter a testing mode: it writes a test plan for the main end-to-end flow, then once CI is green records a video of itself running the plan in the browser. The page calls the recording a quick sanity check.

verify-keeps-going.name: Auto-Fix
verify-keeps-going.summary: Devin iterates in its own environment until tests pass before submitting a PR, and the page says Auto-Fix lets it respond to review comments and CI failures until the PR is merge-ready. The in-session loop is set up by the prompt; no retry cap is documented.

loop-starts-next.name: Automations
loop-starts-next.summary: An automation fires on a trigger (schedule, ticket, GitHub, Slack or webhook) and starts a session with a saved prompt. A finished session choosing the next ticket by itself is not documented.
loop-starts-next.short: A schedule + An event or label (Automations)

loop-includes-plan.omitted: Pages checked: Automations, Linear, Jira, Using Playbooks, gallery bulk-plan-backlog and prd-to-tickets (docs.devin.ai). None states whether a plan step runs inside the automation loop, or whether a person approves one first.

design-reads.name: CLI Plan mode
design-reads.summary: Devin CLI's Plan mode profile has only read-only tools (grep, glob, read, todo, question, exit-plan), so it can look at the code but not change it.

design-form.name: CLI Plan mode
design-form.summary: The plan is written to a file that always opens with a heading and a summary paragraph; nothing beyond those is documented.
design-form.short: Plan file; heading and summary only

design-reuse.omitted: Pages checked: Commands & Flags, Essential Commands, Changelog (Stable) (docs.devin.ai). They do not say the CLI plan names reused code, risks or breaking changes; only a 'megaplan' keyword that makes it ask a clarifying question.

design-approval.name: CLI Plan mode
design-approval.summary: Leaving Plan mode shows an approval prompt with three choices: implement and accept edits, implement and bypass permissions, or plan needs changes.
design-approval.short: Approval prompt on leaving Plan mode

design-tasks.omitted: Pages checked: Commands & Flags, Essential Commands, Changelog (Stable), Subagents (docs.devin.ai). The plan profile has a todo tool, but no page says the plan is split into tasks or stored beyond the plan file.

demoable.summary: The Free self-serve plan lists limited Devin usage, plus access to Devin Review and DeepWiki.

plan-name.name: Spec Mode
plan-name.summary: The Interaction Modes page offers Spec Mode, which plans before implementation: Droid investigates and proposes a plan before any code changes. Missions, a separate mode, coordinate larger multi-feature work with an orchestrator.

execute-name.name: Worker session
execute-name.summary: In a Mission, each feature gets a fresh worker session with clean context, and the page uses 'workers' for the same thing.

plan-hitl.name: Specification Mode
plan-hitl.summary: Droid researches read-only and proposes a plan; nothing is edited until the person approves, and the person can approve or keep iterating on it. In Missions, execution starts once the plan is approved.

plan-persist.name: Specification Mode
plan-persist.summary: Once approved, the plan can optionally be saved as a dated Markdown file (default .factory/docs). Whether Spec Mode splits it into separate tasks is not documented.
plan-persist.short: Yes: Spec Mode can save a file

plan-contents.name: Missions plan
plan-contents.summary: A Mission plan is features grouped into milestones, and each feature has its own validation criteria visible in the Factory App. Explicit dependency edges between features are not documented (ordering is mentioned).
plan-contents.short: Mixed: Missions criteria; dependencies not documented

verify-judge.name: Validation workers
verify-judge.summary: Validation workers run at the end of each milestone, verifying its work, and Missions validate their own work by exercising the running application.

verify-runs-app.name: User-testing validation
verify-runs-app.summary: Missions validate their own work by exercising the running application; each feature is checked by user-facing QA against the running app, which needs a script that can start or mock the app.
verify-runs-app.short: Yes, QA against the running app

verify-keeps-going.name: Stop hook
verify-keeps-going.summary: A user-written hook runs when Droid is about to finish; a block decision with a reason keeps it working, so a script can require a check before it stops. Not a built-in loop: plain sessions and droid exec are not documented as retrying.

loop-starts-next.name: Mission orchestrator
loop-starts-next.summary: After each feature or milestone finishes, the orchestrator starts the next work from the plan. Separately, scheduled automations (for example the "Ticket to PR" starter, every 15 minutes) pick up ready tickets.
loop-starts-next.short: A finished run + A schedule (Missions, automations)

loop-includes-plan.name: Missions plan approval
loop-includes-plan.summary: A Mission's plan is built with the person and must be approved before execution starts; the docs describe the orchestrator working from that plan and do not describe it re-planning during execution.
loop-includes-plan.short: No: plan approved before it runs

design-reads.name: Spec Mode
design-reads.summary: Spec Mode is read-only: Droid searches the repo, reads files, inspects linked artifacts and asks questions, and changes nothing until the plan is approved.

design-form.name: Spec Mode
design-form.summary: A concrete implementation plan is shown for review; it can optionally be saved as a Markdown file once a setting is on. No fixed template is shown.

design-reuse.name: Spec Mode
design-reuse.summary: Reuse comes only if the person asks: the docs advise naming existing patterns in the request, but no page says the plan must list reuse, risks or breaking changes.

design-approval.name: Spec Mode
design-approval.summary: When the plan is ready Droid calls an exit-spec-mode tool to ask for approval; the person then proceeds or keeps iterating.

design-tasks.omitted: Pages checked: Interaction Modes, Droid CLI Quickstart, Droid CLI Reference, Custom droids (docs.factory.com). After approval the same session implements the plan; no page says it is split into stored tasks.

plan-name.omitted: Pages checked: Research, plan and iterate; About Copilot cloud agent; the 2026-04-01 changelog post (docs.github.com, github.blog). They describe asking for a plan before changes, but none names the planning feature; 'Research, plan and iterate' is a how-to page title.

execute-name.name: Copilot cloud agent
execute-name.summary: The docs say Copilot cloud agent can research a repository, plan changes, and implement them in the background.

plan-hitl.name: Research, plan and iterate
plan-hitl.summary: The cloud agent shows a plan before making changes; the person reviews it and iterates with follow-up prompts until it matches their intent, then asks it to implement. In Copilot CLI plan mode the person chooses to accept the plan before autopilot starts.
plan-hitl.short: Yes: review and iterate on the plan

plan-persist.omitted: Pages checked (docs.github.com): Research, plan and iterate; Copilot CLI autopilot; Copilot on GitHub.com; Best practices; Dynamic workflows. They say the plan is shown in the conversation or executed by the same session; none says it is saved as a file or tracker items.

plan-contents.omitted: Pages checked (docs.github.com): Research, plan and iterate; Copilot CLI autopilot; Best practices; improve-a-project tutorial. None says a plan is split into tasks carrying acceptance criteria or dependencies (the tutorial has the person check criteria on issues Copilot creates from findings, which is not plan output).

verify-judge.name: Cloud agent session
verify-judge.summary: The agent works in its own GitHub Actions environment, where it runs tests and linters to validate changes. How the results decide whether it keeps going before opening the PR is not documented.

verify-runs-app.omitted: Pages checked: Managing agent sessions, Using cloud agent on GitHub, Best practices for the cloud agent (docs.github.com). They say the agent runs tests and linters and can build and validate in its environment, but none says it starts the app or drives it as a user.

verify-keeps-going.name: agentStop hook
verify-keeps-going.summary: An agentStop hook fires when the agent finishes; its output can set decision block with a reason, which forces another agent turn. A built-in rule that the cloud agent keeps retrying until a check passes is not documented.

loop-starts-next.name: Copilot automations
loop-starts-next.summary: A saved task runs when a trigger fires: a recurring schedule, an issue created, a pull request opened, or a pull request synchronized. Picking the next ready issue by itself is not documented for automations.
loop-starts-next.short: A schedule + An event or label (automations)

loop-includes-plan.omitted: Pages checked: About automations, Creating automations, Managing rationale and approvals, Using cloud agent on GitHub (docs.github.com). None states whether a plan step runs inside the automation loop or is approved before it.

design-reads.name: Plan mode
design-reads.summary: The plan agent researches the task with read-only tools and codebase analysis to find requirements and constraints, and makes no code change until the plan is approved.

design-form.name: Plan mode
design-form.summary: A plan draft in a standard format shown in the chat: summary, breakdown of steps and open questions. It can be opened as a Markdown file.
design-form.short: Chat plan; can open as Markdown

design-reuse.name: Plan mode
design-reuse.summary: Constraints are named during research and ambiguity becomes open questions; reuse and breaking changes are not documented.

design-approval.name: Plan mode
design-approval.summary: Nothing changes until the person reviews and approves the plan, then clicks Start Implementation.

design-tasks.name: Plan mode
design-tasks.summary: The plan's steps are the units of work and there is no separate task store; Start Implementation hands the plan to an agent session.

plan-name.name: GitHub Issue Triage
plan-name.summary: The Software Factory page names the triage automation GitHub Issue Triage: it prioritizes issues, checks dependencies and establishes acceptance criteria before applying ready-for-dev.

execute-name.name: GitHub Issue to PR
execute-name.summary: The Software Factory page names the developer automation GitHub Issue to PR; it watches the ready-for-dev trigger label and opens pull requests.

plan-hitl.name: Software Factory triage
plan-hitl.summary: The triage agent runs as an automation that checks every 5 minutes: it prioritizes issues, checks dependencies, establishes acceptance criteria, then applies the ready-for-dev label. The page describes no step where a person approves or edits the result; the person writes the issues and acceptance criteria beforehand.

plan-persist.name: ready-for-dev label
plan-persist.summary: The output of triage is the GitHub issue carrying the ready-for-dev label, which the developer automation watches. A separate task list or plan file is not documented.

plan-contents.name: Software Factory triage
plan-contents.summary: The triage agent checks the issue's dependencies and establishes acceptance criteria before applying ready-for-dev. How the criteria are written is not documented.
plan-contents.short: Yes: triage checks dependencies and criteria

verify-judge.name: Goal Completion Loop
verify-judge.summary: In the SDK, a second judge LLM audits the transcript for evidence, such as test output, that proves the objective is complete. The Issue to PR automation lists running tests as a step but does not document what happens when they fail.

verify-runs-app.name: QA agent
verify-runs-app.summary: The QA agent (a GitHub Actions plugin, or the /qa-changes skill) runs the changed software rather than the test suite and posts a PASS, FAIL or PARTIAL report as a PR comment. It works from the PR after it is open.

verify-keeps-going.name: Goal Completion Loop
verify-keeps-going.summary: After each agent run the judge decides whether the objective is provably complete; if not, the agent is re-prompted with what is missing and runs again, up to a cap, after which the result is capped.

loop-starts-next.name: Software Factory
loop-starts-next.summary: Four automations poll every 5 minutes. GitHub labels and statuses are the queue, and the next labeled issue is taken at the next poll.

loop-includes-plan.name: Software Factory triage
loop-includes-plan.summary: The triage automation runs on the same 5-minute poll: it prioritizes issues, checks dependencies and establishes acceptance criteria before applying the ready-for-dev label, which triggers the developer automation. No person approves in between.

design-reads.name: Planning agent
design-reads.summary: In the SDK example the planning agent gets only file search, content search and an editor limited to writing PLAN.md, so it can look at the code but not change it.

design-form.name: Planning agent
design-form.summary: A file, PLAN.md, written to a fixed outline in the planning agent's system prompt: objective, context, approach with rationale, and steps.

design-reuse.name: Planning agent
design-reuse.summary: The outline asks for relevant components, constraints and the rationale for the approach; reuse of existing code and breaking changes are not documented.

design-approval.omitted: Pages checked: Creating Custom Agent, Task Tool Set, File-Based Agents, Ask Oracle (docs.openhands.dev). The example script runs the execution agent straight after planning with no pause, which is how the sample is written, not a stated policy.

design-tasks.name: Planning agent
design-tasks.summary: PLAN.md is the handoff: the second agent is told to read it and implement every component. There is no task list beyond the plan's own step list.
design-tasks.short: PLAN.md step list is the handoff

demoable.summary: The GitHub repository states an MIT license and says agents can be run locally, in Docker, on VMs, or anywhere an agent server backend runs.

plan-name.name: Plan Mode
plan-name.summary: The Plan Mode page says Plan Mode creates detailed implementation plans before writing any code.

execute-name.name: Cloud Agents
execute-name.summary: The Cloud Agents page describes cloud agents as running in isolated VMs with full development environments instead of on your local machine.

plan-hitl.name: Plan Mode
plan-hitl.summary: The agent writes a plan that the person reviews and edits in chat or as markdown, then clicks Build when satisfied. If it is not right, the docs advise reverting and refining the plan rather than patching a bad build with follow-ups.
plan-hitl.short: Yes: edit the plan, then Build

plan-persist.name: Plan Mode
plan-persist.summary: The plan opens as an editable virtual file saved by default in the person's home directory; Save to workspace moves it into the repo for sharing.
plan-persist.short: Yes: plan file; Save to workspace

plan-contents.omitted: Pages checked (cursor.com): Plan Mode docs and help, Agent overview, Prompting agents, Agentic coding help, Multi-agent help, Projects. None says plan steps carry acceptance criteria. Multi-agent help says Build in Parallel keeps dependent steps in order but not how dependencies are written.

verify-judge.name: CI auto-fix
verify-judge.summary: Cloud agents automatically try to fix CI failures in PRs they create, and the repository's own CI checks are the judge. A fixed pre-delivery gate that always runs is not documented.

verify-runs-app.name: Cloud Agents
verify-runs-app.summary: The cloud agent works in a cloud VM and can build, test and interact with the changed software, controlling a desktop and browser.
verify-runs-app.short: Yes, in the cloud agent VM

verify-keeps-going.name: stop hook
verify-keeps-going.summary: Cloud agents run the stop and subagentStop hooks, which the help page says let you build self-correcting loops, and automatically try to fix CI failures in PRs they create (switch off with @cursor autofix off).

loop-starts-next.name: Automations
loop-starts-next.summary: A trigger (schedule, source-control, Slack, webhook, Linear event) starts a cloud agent with a saved prompt. One run starting the next is not documented as chaining.
loop-starts-next.short: A schedule + An event or label (Automations)

loop-includes-plan.name: Projects coordinator
loop-includes-plan.summary: The Project coordinator plans the work, delegates it to agents and brings the finished work back; with subscriptions it delegates a fix each time a bug is posted. The page does not say whether each event gets a fresh plan or whether a plan needs approval.
loop-includes-plan.short: Yes: Project coordinator plans and delegates

design-reads.name: Plan Mode
design-reads.summary: The agent asks clarifying questions, then researches the codebase with file, directory and pattern search before it writes the plan.

design-form.name: Plan Mode
design-form.summary: The plan opens as a virtual file you can read and edit, and can be saved into the repo. No fixed template is given.

design-reuse.omitted: Pages checked: Plan Mode, Plan mode help, Agent overview, Prompting agents, Using Agent in CLI (cursor.com). They do not say the plan lists reused code, risks or breaking changes.

design-approval.name: Plan Mode
design-approval.summary: The person reviews and edits the plan, then clicks Build; the page frames the mode as approving the approach first.
design-approval.short: Review and edit, then click Build

design-tasks.name: Plan Mode
design-tasks.summary: One plan and one Build click; Build in Parallel runs independent steps at once and keeps dependent steps in order. No separate task records are described.
design-tasks.short: One plan; independent steps in parallel

demoable.summary: The docs say Cloud Agents require a paid Cursor plan and are charged at API pricing for the selected model.

plan-name.name: Plan mode
plan-name.summary: The permission modes page describes plan mode: Claude researches and proposes changes without editing source, entered with Shift+Tab or a /plan prefix.

execute-name.name: Session
execute-name.summary: The docs describe each Claude Code conversation as a session, with its own context window, where Claude gathers context, acts and verifies.

plan-hitl.name: Plan mode
plan-hitl.summary: Claude writes a plan and does not edit source files until it is approved. The person can open the plan in a text editor (Ctrl+G) and edit it; approving offers three choices: continue in auto mode, continue approving each edit, or keep planning.
plan-hitl.short: Yes: edit it, approve, or keep planning

plan-persist.name: Agent teams
plan-persist.summary: In an agent team the lead creates tasks in a shared task list, stored locally under ~/.claude/tasks/{team-name}/. Agent teams are experimental and off by default.
plan-persist.short: Yes: agent teams task list on disk

plan-contents.name: Agent teams
plan-contents.summary: Tasks in the shared task list can depend on other tasks: a pending task with unresolved dependencies cannot be claimed until they are completed. Acceptance criteria on a task are not documented.
plan-contents.short: Mixed: agent teams have dependencies; criteria undocumented

verify-judge.name: /goal
verify-judge.summary: After every turn a separate small model checks the condition. The evaluator runs no commands and reads no files, so the condition must be something the transcript shows, such as a test result the agent's own check produced.

verify-runs-app.omitted: Pages checked: Best practices, Common workflows, Run Claude Code programmatically, Use Claude Code in the cloud (code.claude.com). They advise asking for evidence such as test output or a screenshot but do not document Claude Code starting the app and driving it as a built-in step.

verify-keeps-going.name: /goal
verify-keeps-going.summary: After every turn a model checks the condition; if it is not met, Claude starts another turn using the evaluator's reason as guidance. The loop ends when the condition is met, judged impossible, or cleared by the person.

loop-starts-next.name: Agent teams
loop-starts-next.summary: In an agent team, a teammate that finishes a task picks up the next unassigned, unblocked task from the shared list on its own. Experimental and off by default.

loop-includes-plan.name: Agent teams
loop-includes-plan.summary: The team lead creates the tasks in the shared task list (with dependencies) and teammates work through them. The page does not say a person approves that task list first.
loop-includes-plan.short: Yes: team lead writes the task list

design-reads.name: Plan mode
design-reads.summary: Claude reads files and runs shell commands to explore and does not edit source; edits stay blocked until a plan is approved (with a stated exception for bypass permissions in an interactive terminal).

design-form.name: Plan mode
design-form.summary: A plan written to a file and shown for review; you can open it in your editor and change it before approving. Required sections are not documented.
design-form.short: Editable plan file; no required sections

design-reuse.name: Plan mode
design-reuse.summary: Not built in: the docs' example prompt asks which files change, and guidance says to point Claude at an existing pattern, so reuse comes from what you ask for.

design-approval.name: Plan mode
design-approval.summary: When the plan is ready Claude presents it and offers to approve (auto mode or review each edit) or keep planning.
design-approval.short: Approve, review each edit, or keep planning

design-tasks.omitted: Pages checked: Permission modes, Best practices, Common workflows, Tools reference, Interactive mode (code.claude.com). Approving ends plan mode and Claude edits in the same session; no page says the plan is split into tasks.

destination.summary: The overview points to parallel subagents, background agents, scheduled Routines and the Agent SDK for custom orchestration.

queue.name: Issues, Projects, Cycles
queue.summary: Issues are Linear's fundamental unit of work; Projects group issues around a shared outcome, and Cycles are a team's repeating planning period.

queue.name: Work items (formerly issues)
queue.summary: Work items are the building blocks of Jira and can represent a story, bug, task or another work type.

queue.name: Issues, sub-issues, Projects
queue.summary: Issues track bugs, features and ideas; sub-issues add hierarchies between issues, and Projects is integrated with issues to plan and track a team's work.
